newsitem.title: USA: Intel seen in price strategy for Klamath.
newsitem.headline: Intel seen in price strategy for Klamath.

text.p: While Intel Corp is the comfortable position of having almost no competition for all but its cheapest microprocessors, the playing field is about to become more crowded.

Price cuts announced this week might reflect the industry leader's strategy for dealing with the fresh competition, notably a pre-emptive challenge to Intel's yet-to-be-released Klamath chip, analysts said.
This spring Advanced Micro Devices Inc plans to beat Klamath to market with its K6 sixth-generation multimedia chip, while Cyrix Corp will release a similar product.
"What makes this pricing (by Intel) most unusual is, in contrast to prievious price cuts, they are much more targeted, more tactical and opportunistic," said Drew Peck of Cowen & Co.
"What is different this time is they are about to see serious competition, and they are not interested in engaging in a price war (with Klamath) if they can help it," he said.
Every quarter, Intel typically cuts prices on a majority of its microprocessors, but it surprised some observers this week by making no change in its Pentium Pro prices.
The cuts published this week range up to 34 percent on Intel's 133 megahertz Pentium, its mainstream consumer chip.
In Peck's opinion, Intel opened a wide gap between its Pentium Pros and Pentium prices so it could position the Klamath in the middle, with room to adjust depending on competition.
Intel's Karen Alter, director of microprocessor marketing and business planning, said Pentium Pro prices were not cut this time because of sharp reductions during 1996.
"Pentium Pro prices are exactly where they should be in a product's life cycle," Alter said.

"We priced very aggressively compared to what we would normally do with a ramping up-product," Alter said, referring to the Pentium Pro's first year in 1996. "We wanted to help customers get systems into the marketplace."

"I personally think they are not cutting Pentium Pro because early on they'll be moving the market toward the Klamath," Edelstone said. "Intel wouldn't want industry spending lot of time developing systems for the Pentium Pro when the Klamath is coming out."
By holding Pentium Pro prices steady, Intel also could have given more freedom to Advanced Micro on pricing its K6 chip, heading off the threat of a price war between the companies, Peck said.
Intel stock rose 5-3/8 to 160-1/8 in Nasdaq trading on Thursday.
